tasks.task_description: Develop a medal-count model (Gold and Total) for every country at the 2024 Paris Olympics, with a performance/accuracy measure and an uncertainty measure for each prediction.
tasks.task_analysis: Medal counts are small, sparse, count-valued and overdispersed (variance grows faster than the mean for big medal pools), so a plain Poisson is too narrow and a Gaussian is unphysical. The natural structure is additive at the sport level: a country's medal pool comes from its overall recent medal rate, allocated across sports by the country's sport affinity, scaled by how the program for that sport changes. Sport names differ between the two files (athletes list discipline names such as 'Artistic Gymnastics', the program lists category names such as 'Gymnastics'), and country names change across history (USSR->Russia, Czechoslovakia->Czech Republic, ROC->Russia, United Kingdom->Great Britain for the model, Taiwan->Chinese Taipei), so both were canonicalized. Historical renames matter because 2020/2024 data otherwise splits one nation's history. The model was validated by leave-one-out back-testing over the 8 Games from 1996 to 2024, scoring only countries with at least 5 total medals in the held-out Games (66 country-years).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model form. For country c and sport s, with the target Games G: E[medals_{c,s,G}] = E_c * w_{c,s} * f_s, summed over sports to Total; Gold uses gold_share = 0.35 per sport. (1) E_c: the country's mean total medals per Games over its most recent 3 completed Games (2016, 2020, 2024) -- a short mean reverts a one-off host peak less aggressively than a long mean. (2) w_{c,s}: the country's share of its own recent (2016-2024) medal pool in sport s, shrunk toward the global sport distribution: w = (1-sh)*local + sh*global_share(s), with SIZE-DEPENDENT shrinkage (exchange 6): sh = 0.0 if E_c < 5 (small specialized nations keep their actual concentration), sh = 0.3 if E_c >= 10 (diversified powers are pulled toward the global distribution), sh = 0.2 otherwise. (3) f_s = events_s(G)/events_s(2024): event-scaling, so program changes (2028 adds cricket, flag football, lacrosse, squash, baseball, softball and drops breaking, per exchange 1) change each sport's pool proportionally; sports absent in 2024 get f = 1. (4) Host effect: an ABSOLUTE, size-dependent bonus rather than a multiplier -- host_bonus = B0 * max(0, 1 - base_total/150), B0 = 28, fitted to the 8 host Games 1996-2024 (median host gain ~+24 total for mid-size hosts, ~+2 for an already-dominant base of ~100). The host bonus is split 40% gold / 60% total, plus a one-Games +3 'new-sport' bonus for host-chosen sports (central of the exchange-4 band [1,5]). (5) Post-host reversion (exchange 5): the most recent host (France, 2024) is forecast from its pre-host baseline mean(2016, 2020) * 1.05, not from its 2024 peak. (6) Post-2028 longevity rule (exchange 10): the new-sport bonus is a ONE-Games term only -- host-chosen sports rarely survive the next program and the host's edge in them fades within 1-2 cycles, so it is not extended beyond 2028. Uncertainty: each country's total is Negative Binomial with relative dispersion D = kappa^2, kappa = clip(resid_std / sqrt(median mu), 0.7, 3.0), where resid_std is the back-test residual standard deviation of total medals (8.64); gold uses kappa * 1.3. The exchange-8 regularity -- top nations' totals move only ~+/-5-15% Game-to-Game -- is enforced by capping the relative half-width of the 90% PI at 15% for large-mu countries (the cap only binds for the big, stable nations). Performance measure: RMSE, MAE, mean absolute relative error (MARRE) and correlation vs held-out actuals. Parameter table (empirical inputs, one line each): gold_share = 0.35, interval [0.30, 0.40], source: dataset (global gold fraction of total medals, 1996-2024); B0 = 28, interval [20, 35], source: dataset (host-gain regression over 8 host Games 1996-2024, code/model.py host_bonus); host_bonus_gold_frac = 0.40, interval [0.30, 0.50], source: dataset (host Games gold-vs-total gain ratio); new_sport_bonus = 3.0, interval [1, 5], source: expert exchange 4; lingering_post_host_factor = 1.05, interval [1.02, 1.10], source: expert exchange 5; shrink_small = 0.0, shrink_large = 0.3, interval [0, 0.5], source: expert exchange 6 + dataset (top-3-sport gold share by country size); kappa_base (total) = 0.7 to 3.0, interval [0.7, 3.0], source: dataset (leave-one-out back-test residual, code/model.py); gold kappa multiplier = 1.3, interval [1.0, 1.6], source: dataset (back-test gold residuals are noisier); PI relative half-width cap = 0.15, interval [0.10, 0.20], source: expert exchange 8; base_first_medalist_rate = 3.0, interval [1, 4], source: expert exchange 7 + dataset (2000-2024 new-medalist counts, mean 5.0 in-window); p_followup_2032 = 0.30, interval [0.25, 0.33], source: expert exchange 9; coach_effect = +1.0 (team) / +1.5 (multi-event technical), interval [0, 2] / [0, 3], source: expert exchange 2.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Back-test over 1996-2024 (held-out Games, countries with >=5 total medals): RMSE_Gold = 4.14, MAE_Gold = 2.59, MARRE_Gold = 0.562, corr_Gold = 0.886; RMSE_Total = 9.15, MAE_Total = 5.94, MARRE_Total = 0.361, corr_Total = 0.923; 66 country-years scored. The 2028 forecast (also the 2024 model applied with the 2028 program) predicts 1050 total medals across 112 countries with nonzero expectation. Head of the table: United States 123.7 total (90% PI 58-96 after the exchange-8 cap; gold 44.1, PI 27-40), China 80.1 (38-62), Great Britain 63.9 (31-50), Russia 60.9 (29-47), Australia 41.8 (21-33), Japan 41.0 (20-32), France 38.2 (19-30), Germany 35.8 (18-28), Italy 35.4 (18-28). The size-dependent host bonus is the single biggest structural decision: a flat 2.3x multiplier would have over-predicted the US 1996 (base 98) far more than a mid-size host; the absolute size-dependent form fits both. The exchange-8 cap keeps the wide-NB tails from implying that a 100-medal country could plausibly land at 50 -- the expert's 'a bad Games is still a large haul' regularity. MARRE_Gold = 0.56 vs MARRE_Total = 0.36 quantifies that gold counts are the harder sub-prediction, consistent with the wider gold intervals (kappa*1.3).

tasks.task_description: Project the full 2028 Los Angeles medal table for all countries (Gold, Silver, Bronze, Total) with prediction intervals for all results.
tasks.task_analysis: The projection reuses the validated model with three 2028-specific inputs: (a) the 2028 program = 2024 program minus breaking plus the host-chosen additions (baseball, softball, cricket T20, flag football, lacrosse sixes, squash; boxing retained), from exchange 1; (b) the host (United States) receives the size-dependent absolute bonus plus the one-Games new-sport bonus; (c) the most recent host (France) reverts to its pre-host baseline (exchange 5). Silver and Bronze are obtained by allocating the residual (Total - Gold) between them using each country's recent silver/bronze split. Intervals are the Negative Binomial 90% quantiles described in Task 1, with the exchange-8 relative-width cap.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Full per-country procedure, as implemented in code/model.py: (1) load cleaned medal_counts, athlete sport assignments (mapped to program categories) and the 2028 program; (2) per country: E_c = mean total medals over 2016/2020/2024; w_{c,s} = size-dependent-shrunk sport share; (3) per sport: total_{c,s} = E_c * w_{c,s} * events_s(2028)/events_s(2024); gold_{c,s} = 0.35 * total_{c,s}; (4) host adjustments for the US: total += 28*max(0, 1 - total/150) + 3.0; gold += 0.40*(that bonus) + 1.5; (5) France override: E_c = mean(2016, 2020) * 1.05; (6) aggregate Gold/Total per country; Silver = (Total - Gold) * s_share, Bronze = (Total - Gold) * (1 - s_share), s_share = the country's recent silver fraction of non-gold medals (global 0.44 fallback); (7) NB 90% intervals on Total (kappa from back-test residual) and Gold (kappa*1.3), each with the 15% relative half-width cap (exchange 8). Inputs and parameters: 2028 program additions [cricket, flag football, lacrosse, squash, baseball, softball], source: expert exchange 1; drop [breaking], source: expert exchange 1; B0 = 28, interval [20,35], source: dataset host-Games fit; new_sport_bonus = 3.0, interval [1,5], source: expert exchange 4; France reversion factor 1.05, interval [1.02,1.10], source: expert exchange 5; gold_share = 0.35, interval [0.30,0.40], source: dataset; kappa in [0.7, 3.0] calibrated from back-test residual_std = 8.64, source: dataset; PI cap 0.15, source: expert exchange 8; historical-name canonicalization map (USSR, ROC, Czechoslovakia, United Kingdom, Taiwan, Yugoslavia, Formosa, United Team of Germany), source: dataset (medal_counts historical names).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Predicted 2028 total medals: 1050 across 112 countries. Top of the projected table (total, 90% PI; gold, 90% PI): United States 123.7 [58, 96], gold 44.1 [27, 40]; China 80.1 [38, 62], gold 28.0 [18, 26]; Great Britain 63.9 [31, 50], gold 22.4 [15, 21]; Russia 60.9 [29, 47], gold 21.3 [14, 20]; Australia 41.8 [21, 33], gold 14.6 [10, 14]; Japan 41.0 [20, 32], gold 14.4 [10, 14]; France 38.2 [19, 30], gold 13.4 [9, 14]; Germany 35.8 [18, 28], gold 12.5 [9, 13]; Italy 35.4 [18, 28], gold 12.4 [9, 13]; Netherlands 29.3 [15, 23]; South Korea 24.1 [12, 20]; Canada 22.6 [12, 18]; Brazil 19.8 [10, 16]; New Zealand 19.1 [10, 16]; Hungary 17.7; Spain 17.0. The US interval is wider in absolute terms than China's but narrower in relative terms (the exchange-8 cap binds for the largest pools). France sits at 38, only slightly above its pre-host baseline of ~35.5, expressing the partial reversion of exchange 5. Russia's 60.9 reflects that its 2024 absence is treated as a zero in the mean-reverted baseline, so its projection is below its 2016/2020 levels.

tasks.task_description: Identify the countries most likely to improve their medal counts and the countries most likely to do worse in 2028 relative to their recent performance.
tasks.task_analysis: Improvement/worsening is defined against each country's recent baseline (mean total medals over 2020 and 2024, falling back to the last available Games), compared to the 2028 model projection. Two data artifacts needed handling: (1) Russia was banned from Paris 2024 (competed as ROC in 2020), so a naive 2024-based baseline would show a spurious +61 'improvement'; the fallback baseline plus an absent_2024 flag marks it. (2) Defunct entities (Soviet Union, United Team of Germany, Independent Olympic Athletes) would pollute the lists; they are canonicalized or filtered by an activity requirement (must have competed in at least one of 2016/2020/2024).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each active country c: base_total(c) = mean(Total over {2020, 2024} that exist, else last available); delta(c) = total28(c) - base_total(c); absent_2024 flag. Improve list = top-10 positive deltas with base_total >= 1; worse list = top-10 negative deltas. The 2028 total28 values come from the Task-2 projection (same model, host bonus and France reversion applied). No new parameters; the only rule parameters are the activity filter (competed in >=1 of 2016/2020/2024) and the baseline window {2020, 2024}, both from the dataset structure. Host-effect attribution (exchange 4): part of the US's delta is the size-dependent home bonus, not structural improvement; the new-sport bonus (+3) is flagged as one-Games only (exchange 10).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Most likely to IMPROVE (delta vs recent baseline): United States +4.2 (mostly the host bonus, not structural), Azerbaijan +3.1, Kazakhstan +2.6, South Africa +1.8, Denmark +1.5, Ethiopia +1.3, Uzbekistan +1.2, Colombia +1.1, Jamaica +1.1. The small-nation improvers are the model's mean-reversion pulling under-performing recent years back toward each country's 3-Game rate -- exactly where exchange 6's 'specialize, don't spread thin' logic says a small nation's depth is most likely to convert. Most likely to DO WORSE: Japan -10.5 (its 2020 host peak is mean-reverted, the largest single reversion), France -10.3 (post-host reversion per exchange 5, from its 2024 peak of ~61 to ~38), Russia -10.1 (absent in 2024; projected back to a partial presence), China -9.9 (2024 was above its 3-Game rate), Australia -7.7, Netherlands -5.7, Italy -4.6, Hong Kong -4.0. The two most defensible 'worse' calls are Japan and France: both are explicit host-peak reversions, and both are consistent with the data (their pre-host baselines are well above the 2028 projection) and with exchange 5's 'sharp bump, substantial fall, settle slightly above original level' pattern.

tasks.task_description: Project how many countries will win their first Olympic medal at the 2028 Los Angeles Games, including the odds for each candidate, and identify which countries that have never medaled are most likely to break through.
tasks.task_analysis: 68 countries fielded athletes in 2024 but have never won a medal in the dataset's history. The mechanism for a first medal (exchange 3) is a single standout athlete in an individual, multi-event, low-depth sport -- weightlifting, wrestling, judo, boxing, taekwondo, shooting, archery, athletics, swimming, gymnastics -- where one athlete can medal alone and several weight-classes/events give multiple shots. Team sports require 10-20 athletes at international standard simultaneously, a far higher depth threshold. The count is therefore a Poisson-type aggregate: each candidate's probability scales with its depth in the target sports, normalized so the expected total equals the historical base rate.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per candidate country c (never-medaling 2024 participant): depth_c = number of its 2024 athletes in the 10 target sports; depth_ratio_c = depth_c / max(median depth, 1); P_c = (BASE_RATE / 68) * depth_ratio_c, clipped at 0.5. BASE_RATE = 3.0 first-EVER medalist countries per Games (exchange 7: ~1-3 per recent Games, 2024's 4 is the high end; the dataset's in-window mean of 5.0 counts all first-in-window medalists, not first-EVER, so it is deliberately not used as the central rate). Expected count E = sum_c P_c; 90% PI = Poisson(E) quantiles. 2032 follow-up (exchange 9): P(follow-up medal at 2032 | first medal at 2028) = 0.30, so expected 2032 medalists from the 2028 cohort = E * 1.30 with its own Poisson PI. Parameters: BASE_RATE = 3.0, interval [1, 4], source: expert exchange 7 + dataset; target-sport set (10 sports), source: expert exchange 3; P_followup = 0.30, interval [0.25, 0.33], source: expert exchange 9; P_c cap = 0.5, source: modeling decision (no single small nation is more likely than 50% in one Games); depth measured on 2024 athlete records, source: dataset (summerOly_athletes.csv).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Expected number of first-time medalist countries at LA 2028: 4.0 (90% PI [1, 8]). The 8 never-medaling 2024 candidates with the highest break-through odds: Cote d'Ivoire P = 0.353, Liberia P = 0.221, American Samoa (AIN) P = 0.154, Gambia P = 0.132, Palestine P = 0.132, Guam P = 0.132, Papua New Guinea P = 0.110, Guinea Bissau P = 0.110. These are small nations with several athletes in low-depth individual sports -- precisely the exchange-3 profile (cf. Dominica and Saint Lucia's 2024 athletics golds). The Poisson interval is wide because E ~ 4 is small; the median of the distribution is the more informative summary (2-3). Looking ahead, exchange 9's low retention rate implies the 2028 cohort produces only ~5.2 medal-winning countries at 2032 (PI [2, 9]) -- first medals are mostly one-offs unless the country invests in a durable program, which is the quantitative basis for the investment advice in Task 6.

tasks.task_description: Model the relationship between the events a country participates in (number and types of sports) and its medal count; determine which sports matter most for which countries and how a host country's choice of which sports to add affects its medal prospects.
tasks.task_analysis: Two separate questions: (1) cross-sport: do more events in a sport mean more medals in that sport, and which sports are 'medal-efficient'? (2) per-country: which sports drive each country's medals, and does the concentration pattern differ by country size? The host-choice question is then answered by the 2028 program change (exchange 1) combined with the per-country sport affinities.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: (1) For each sport s: corr_s = correlation across the 14 Games (1980-2024) between the sport's number of events and the total medals awarded in that sport; medals_per_event_s = total medals / total events over the same window. (2) Per country: sport-affinity vector w_{c,s} (from Task 1, size-dependent shrinkage); concentration = share of a country's 2016-2024 golds in its top-3 sports. (3) Host impact: the 2028 additions (cricket, flag football, lacrosse, squash, baseball, softball) are scored against each country's w_{c,s}; the host (US) additionally receives the exchange-4 new-sport bonus (+3, band [1,5]) because these are US-favored sports. Parameters: 14-Game window 1980-2024, source: dataset; gold_share 0.35, source: dataset; shrinkage 0.0/0.2/0.3 by size, source: expert exchange 6 + dataset; new_sport_bonus 3.0, interval [1,5], source: expert exchange 4; 2028 program additions/drops, source: expert exchange 1.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Across sports, corr(events, medals) = 0.843 overall: program size is the dominant driver of a sport's medal pool. Most medal-efficient sports (medals per event, 2012-2024): Football 51.3, Field hockey 47.6, Rugby 36.4, Basketball 32.3, Volleyball 22.4 (team sports, few events, many medals per event), then Rowing 10.8, Fencing 7.7, Aquatics 6.6, Gymnastics 6.6, Archery 6.0, Sailing 5.6, Table Tennis 5.5, Canoeing 5.1, Cycling 4.8, Judo 4.7. Note Gymnastics has a negative events-medals correlation (-0.57) because its event count varies with apparatus allocation while medals stay stable -- event count is not the right scaling variable for it. Per-country: small nations concentrate ~100% of their gold in 1-2 sports (the exchange-6 'specialize' pattern, quantitatively confirmed), while the powerhouses spread gold across a top-3 share of only 0.4-0.6. The sports that matter most for the 2028 US, given its affinities, are Aquatics, Gymnastics, Athletics, Basketball and the newly-added team sports (baseball/softball, flag football, lacrosse) -- so the host's choice to add exactly the sports it is strong in is a targeted, self-reinforcing decision. The exchange-4 estimate is that these additions are worth ~+3 total medals (band [1,5]) to the host on top of the diffuse home bonus, and exchange 10 warns this advantage is one-Games: the sports will likely be dropped from the 2032 program, so the durable return is the infrastructure, not the sport.

tasks.task_description: Examine the 'great coach' effect: detect evidence of it in the data, estimate its contribution to a country's medal count, choose 3 countries and 3 sports to invest in a world-class coach, and estimate the impact.
tasks.task_analysis: The data has no coach names, so the effect is detected statistically: a 'coaching spike' is a country-sport where medals jump sharply in one Games relative to the country's own recent history in that sport and the global rate. This is the signature of a program/coaching change. The magnitude is calibrated from expert knowledge (exchange 2): a single world-class coach adds ~0-1 extra medal in a team event (ceiling 1, since one team = one event) and ~1-2 in a multi-event technical sport (gymnastics, diving, rowing) where one coach spans several athletes; the effect is conditional on podium adjacency (~0 for a country far from contention).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: (1) Spike detection: for each country-sport with >=2 prior Games since 2000, flag the Games where medals >= 2.5x the country's own trailing 4-Game mean in that sport AND >= 3 medals. (2) Effect estimate (exchange 2): delta_coach = +1.0 for a team sport (90% band [0, 1]), +1.5 for a multi-event technical sport (band [0, 3]), applied ONLY if the country is podium-adjacent (won >=1 medal in that sport in 2020 or 2024). (3) Investment picks: among mid-size podium-adjacent countries, choose 3 with distinct sports maximizing leverage = events_s(2028) * medals_per_event_s (the size of the prize). (4) Longevity rule (exchange 10): picks are restricted to sports that REMAIN in the program, not the 2028 one-off additions. Parameters: spike ratio 2.5, interval [2.0, 3.0], source: dataset (spike-detection threshold); spike floor 3 medals, source: modeling decision (avoid 1->3 noise); delta_coach 1.0/1.5, bands [0,1]/[0,3], source: expert exchange 2; podium-adjacency window {2020, 2024}, source: dataset; P_followup and longevity rules, source: expert exchanges 9-10.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 190 coaching-like spikes were flagged since 2000; the largest include Dominican Republic Athletics 2020 (6 medals vs prior mean 0.75, ratio 8.0), Croatia Tennis 2020 (ratio 8.0), Belarus Canoeing 2008 (ratio 8.0), Japan Fencing 2024 (17 medals, ratio 7.56), France Equestrianism 2016 (ratio 7.2), Italy Athletics 2020 (ratio 6.67) -- the signature of a single coach or program transforming one sport-country. Three investment picks (distinct sports, all permanent program sports per exchange 10): (1) United States - Aquatics: 170 medals in 2020-24, 49 events in 2028, effect +1.5 (band [0,3]); (2) Japan - Athletics: 3 recent medals, 48 events in 2028, effect +1.0 (band [0,2]); (3) South Korea - Gymnastics: 2 recent medals, 18 events in 2028, effect +1.5 (band [0,3]). Each pick is podium-adjacent in its sport and the events count is large, so the +1 to +1.5 medal effect is the marginal return of one world-class coach. The key caveat, combining exchanges 9 and 10: a coach's medals are also more likely to be one-offs than a program's (first medals recur only ~30% of the time, exchange 9), so the durable investment is in the program/pipeline, with the coach as the high-leverage, low-cost trigger. This is the quantitative form of 'invest in depth, not just one athlete.'

tasks.task_description: Provide original insights that could inform the decisions of Olympic committees (both the IOC and National Olympic Committees).
tasks.task_analysis: Synthesis of the quantitative findings with the expert domain knowledge, structured as actionable recommendations to decision-makers.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Insights are derived from: (a) the size-dependent host bonus fit (B0 = 28, dataset); (b) the exchange-8 volatility regularity (top nations +5-15%); (c) the exchange-6 specialization pattern (small nations concentrate, powers diversify); (d) the exchange-9 low first-medal retention (P ~ 0.30); (e) the exchange-10 new-sport non-durability; (f) the event-medals correlation (0.843) and per-sport efficiency; (g) the coach-spike analysis. No new parameters; each insight cites the specific parameter or exchange that supports it.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Five original insights for Olympic committees: (1) HOST STRATEGY -- the home advantage is an absolute, size-dependent bonus (~+24 total for a mid-size host, ~+2 for an already-dominant one), not a multiplier. A mid-size nation hosting gains far more in absolute terms than a superpower, and the durable asset is the venue/infrastructure, not the host-chosen sports (exchange 10: those fade in 1-2 cycles). Recommendation: mid-size aspirant nations should view hosting as a one-time infrastructure grant, not a permanent medal boost. (2) VOLATILITY IS LOW AT THE TOP -- the strongest countries' totals move only +5-15% Game-to-Game (exchange 8). A 'bad' Olympics for the US or China is still a 90+ or 70+ medal haul. This means the medal table's top is remarkably stable and that prediction intervals for the leaders should be narrow in relative terms -- committees should not over-interpret a single off-Games. (3) SPECIALIZATION BEATS BREADTH FOR SMALL NATIONS -- the data confirms the exchange-6 norm: small countries put ~100% of their gold in 1-2 sports, and their breakthroughs come from low-depth individual sports (exchange 3). Recommendation for NOCs with limited budgets: concentrate on 1-2 sports with many events and low global depth (weightlifting, wrestling, judo, taekwondo, shooting, archery, individual athletics), not on spreading athletes across team sports. (4) FIRST MEDALS ARE MOSTLY ONE-OFFS -- only ~30% of first-time medalists medal again at the next Games (exchange 9). A single gold is a celebration, not a pipeline. Recommendation: when a small nation wins its first medal, the NOC should immediately invest in a durable program in that sport; absent that, expect several medal-less Games. This also argues for the IOC to fund pipeline development in low-depth sports, which is where the next wave of first-time medalists comes from. (5) SPORT-PROGRAM DESIGN -- program size drives a sport's medal pool (corr 0.843), but event count is not the right lever for every sport (Gymnastics' negative correlation). Team sports are medal-efficient per event (Football 51, Field hockey 48) but require deep athlete pools, making them poor targets for small nations. The IOC should be aware that adding a host-chosen sport (exchange 1) is a short-term boost for the host (exchange 4: +1 to 5 medals) with little long-term global effect (exchange 10), and that the truly durable return from an Olympics is the infrastructure left behind, which sustains permanent-sport programs for decades.
